questions.question: A patient develops sudden facial droop, unilateral arm weakness, and difficulty speaking. What is the priority FNP action?
choices: Recognize possible stroke and arrange emergency transport/evaluation
Wait to see if symptoms resolve tomorrow
questions.explanation: Sudden focal neurologic deficits are stroke symptoms. Record last-known-well time and arrange emergency evaluation immediately.

questions.question: What does the “T” in B.E. F.A.S.T. emphasize?
choices: Time to call emergency services and document symptom onset
Treat only if symptoms persist 24 hours
questions.explanation: Time matters in stroke. Call emergency services immediately and note when the person was last known well.

questions.question: Why is a TIA an emergency even if symptoms completely resolve?
choices: TIA always causes permanent brain injury
It is a warning sign of future stroke and needs rapid assessment
TIA is only a headache disorder
questions.explanation: Transient focal symptoms can signal temporary brain ischemia and high early stroke risk. Urgent evaluation is required even after resolution.

questions.question: Which headache presentation is a major secondary-headache red flag?
choices: Sudden maximal-at-onset thunderclap headache with vomiting
A chronic unchanged headache with normal exam
questions.explanation: Thunderclap onset is a red flag for hemorrhage or another dangerous secondary cause and requires emergency evaluation.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a seizure?
choices: A normal response to every headache
questions.explanation: A seizure reflects abnormal, excessive, synchronous neuronal activity and may result from epilepsy or an acute medical/neurologic trigger.

questions.question: When should a seizure prompt emergency evaluation?
choices: Only if the patient is embarrassed
If it is a first seizure, lasts 5 minutes or longer, recurs without recovery, or causes breathing difficulty
questions.explanation: First, prolonged, repeated-without-recovery, or complicated seizures need emergency assessment. Airway/breathing and safety are immediate priorities.

questions.question: Which feature best distinguishes delirium from typical dementia?
choices: Delirium is acute and fluctuating with impaired attention
Delirium is always slowly progressive over years
There is never an underlying medical cause
questions.explanation: Delirium is acute, fluctuating brain dysfunction with impaired attention and often an underlying medical trigger; dementia is generally chronic and progressive.

questions.question: An older adult becomes suddenly inattentive and disoriented over hours. What is the best general approach?
choices: Label it dementia based on age
Treat as delirium and urgently evaluate for infection, hypoxia, metabolic disease, medication effects, stroke, and other causes
questions.explanation: Sudden confusion is delirium until proven otherwise. It requires assessment for reversible and dangerous medical causes.

questions.question: Which factor is a major modifiable risk for ischemic stroke?
questions.explanation: Hypertension is a major modifiable stroke risk factor. Diabetes, smoking, dyslipidemia, atrial fibrillation, and vascular disease also contribute.

questions.question: A patient with atrial fibrillation reports a brief episode of unilateral visual loss that resolved. Which mechanism is especially concerning?
choices: Atrial stasis → thrombus → embolic cerebral ischemia/TIA
questions.explanation: AF promotes atrial stasis and thrombus formation. Embolization can cause transient or persistent cerebral ischemia, requiring emergency assessment.
